 2          Stream Trading Corp. files its Original Complaint against Caleb McMeans as follows:
 3                                      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
 4          1.      Stream Trading Corp. was co-founded in early 2024 by two long-time proponents
 5   of blockchain transactions and decentralized finance (“DeFi”).1 In February 2024, Stream Trading
 6   Corp. launched a yield farming protocol (the “Stream Protocol”). While successful, operational
 7   challenges led Stream Trading Corp. to wind down this product by November 2024.
 8          2.      Thereafter, Stream Trading Corp. was approached by Caleb McMeans, who was
 9   known for managing complex yield farming strategies. Mr. McMeans wanted to acquire the Stream
10   Protocol and its brand to help attract customers to his own yield farming strategies. As a result,
11   Stream Trading Corp. and Mr. McMeans began discussing a potential acquisition.
12          3.      In January 2025, discussions with Mr. McMeans culminated in an agreement that
13   transferred the Stream Protocol to Mr. McMeans (the “Agreement”). Under the Agreement, Mr.
14   McMeans also immediately assumed the rights and obligations associated with managing the
15   depositor assets that had remained after the November 2024 winddown as well as any new depositor
16   assets, lenders, and trading strategies. In addition, Stream Trading Corp. permitted Mr. McMeans
17   to use the Stream brand in connection with operating the Stream Protocol.
18          4.      Per the Agreement, after acquiring the Stream Protocol, Mr. McMeans ran it as his
19   own business and exercised complete control over it. He controlled all on-chain trading of
20   cryptocurrencies and off-chain business arrangements (including entering into contracts with
21   various third parties), and he publicly identified himself as the CEO of the Stream Protocol.
22          5.      In early November 2025, the co-founders of Stream Trading Corp. were alarmed to
23   learn that Ryan DeMattia—a yield farming trader employed by Mr. McMeans—had lost
24   approximately $93 million of the Stream Protocol’s assets. This loss represented approximately
25   17.5% of the assets under management by Mr. McMeans through the Stream Protocol and triggered

10   the $93 million loss to the public via the Stream Protocol X account and announce that all
11   withdrawals on Protocol Version 2 would be frozen and new deposits rejected. Mr. McMeans
12   agreed.
13             E.    Mr. McMeans confuses users of the Stream Protocol and parties with whom he

14                   is responsible for performance of obligations owed to them by Mr. McMeans.
15             45.   Unfortunately, Mr. McMeans’s actions in the days that followed did not provide

16   additional clarity to Stream Protocol depositors or third parties with whom Mr. McMeans had

17   contracted since acquiring the Stream Protocol. For example, Mr. McMeans began using the

18   existence of the multi-sig wallet that had only been established because he self-reported suicidal

19   intentions as a basis to argue that he was not in control of the Stream Protocol or its deposits.

20   Instead, he claimed that Stream Trading Corp. was in control. He also began telling third parties

21   with whom he had contracted under the moniker “Stream Trading Company” that the word

22   “Company” was “a typo” and that they should instead deal with Stream Trading Corp. Stream

23   Trading Corp. also discovered that Mr. McMeans had deleted all of his private Discord

24   communications with Mr. DeMattia since October 10, 2025—the same date on which, upon

25   information and belief, Mr. DeMattia experienced liquidation of a significant personal position he

26   held.

27             46.   Mr. McMeans and his lawyer then began asserting a variety of inconsistent and

28   increasingly absurd positions as they tried on a proverbial wardrobe of novel theories. Initially, they
